title: Uncovering Software-Based Power Side-Channel Attacks on Apple M1/M2 Systems
problem: The System Management Controller (SMC) on Apple M1/M2 processors exposes on-chip power meter capabilities through a software interface accessible to unprivileged user-mode applications. This enables software-based power side-channel attacks that can extract sensitive cryptographic data without requiring physical access to the device.
motivation: Software-based power side-channel attacks pose practical security threats to cloud environments and shared systems where traditional side-channel attacks requiring physical access are infeasible.
method: The attack exploits the SMC and its power-related keys to access on-chip power meters from user-space software, analyzing data-dependent power consumption patterns and correlating them with processed data. The researchers demonstrate recovery of AES encryption key bytes from a kernel-mode cryptographic service and examine the feasibility of frequency throttling side-channel attacks on Apple silicon.
key_novelty: First demonstration that software-based power side-channel attacks, previously demonstrated on x86 platforms, are also exploitable on Apple M1/M2 processors through the SMC interface for practical cryptographic key extraction.
contributions: Software-based power side-channel attacks on Apple M1/M2 platforms exploiting SMC
Successful AES key recovery from kernel-mode cryptographic services by unprivileged user-mode code
Analysis of frequency throttling side-channel attack feasibility on Apple silicon
Discussion of countermeasures and implications for on-chip power management interfaces
limitations: Specific limitations of the attack methodology and practical constraints are not discussed in the abstract.
primary_theme: Software-based power side-channel attacks on ARM processors
